title: Chapter 2 – The Chemical Level of Organization
notes: Matter is anything with mass and volume; chemistry studies its structure/interactions.
Elements are pure substances; major biological: O, C, H, N.
Atoms: protons (+), neutrons (0), electrons (−); atomic number = protons; mass number = p+n.
Isotopes vary in neutrons; some are radioactive and decay with characteristic half-lives.
Ions: cations (+) lose electrons; anions (−) gain electrons.
Covalent bonds share electrons; ionic bonds transfer; hydrogen bonds are weak attractions.
Polar vs nonpolar covalent bonds determined by electronegativity differences.
Chemical reactions: synthesis, decomposition, exchange, reversible, redox.
Activation energy is lowered by catalysts; enzymes are biological catalysts.
Energy forms: potential, kinetic, chemical; law of conservation of energy applies.
Water: polarity enables solvent abilities, cohesion, high heat capacity and vaporization.
Solutions, colloids, suspensions differ by particle size and behavior.
Acids (H+ donors), bases (OH− donors), salts (neither); strong vs weak dissociation.
pH is −log[H+]; buffers (carbonic acid–bicarbonate) stabilize pH in body fluids.
Organic molecules contain C/H; functional groups confer properties.
Carbohydrates: mono-, di-, polysaccharides; energy and storage (glycogen).
Lipids: triglycerides, phospholipids (bilayers), steroids; hydrophobic tails, hydrophilic heads.
Proteins: amino acids, peptide bonds, primary→quaternary structure; function depends on shape.
Denaturation disrupts structure and function (temperature, pH).
Enzymes: specificity, active site, induced fit; affected by temp, pH, substrate concentration.
Nucleic acids (DNA/RNA) store and express genetic information.
ATP is the energy currency; generated by catabolic reactions.
Hydrogen bonding in water underlies cohesion and surface tension.
Dehydration synthesis builds polymers; hydrolysis breaks them.
Free radicals have unpaired electrons; antioxidants can neutralize them.
Molarity and percentage describe solution concentration.
Buffers resist pH change by binding/releasing H+ (e.g., H2CO3/HCO3−).
Phospholipids form micelles or bilayers to shield hydrophobic tails from water.
Steroid backbone: four fused rings; cholesterol is a precursor to steroid hormones.
Protein structure levels: primary (sequence), secondary (α-helix/β-sheet), tertiary, quaternary.
